name: Bergson's theory of space and number, and its refutation
plain_explanation: Bergson claims that any idea of number or plurality secretly requires picturing things spread out in space -- but Russell argues this confuses a particular collection of things (like twelve apples) with the abstract number twelve itself, which cannot be pictured at all.
precise_definition: Bergson's claim, from Time and Free Will, that 'every clear idea of number implies a visual image in space,' and that number is 'a collection of units, or... the synthesis of the one and the many' -- a claim Russell argues conflates three distinct things: number in general, a particular number, and a particular collection exemplifying that number.
why_it_mattered: This theory of space is, with the theory of duration, one of the two pillars Bergson's whole system rests on; if it fails, Russell argues, so does Bergson's condemnation of the intellect as inherently 'spatial.'
historical_origin: Set out in Time and Free Will.
examples: Russell's analogy: confusing a particular young man with 'youth,' and 'youth' with the general concept 'period of human life,' then absurdly concluding that the concept 'period of human life' must have two legs
objections: Russell: the confusion of a collection with the number of its terms, and that in turn with number in general, invalidates Bergson's claim that abstract ideas and logic are derived from space
competing_positions: Modern mathematical logic (Frege's and Russell's own definition of number), discussed more fully in the following chapter on logical analysis
